Direct comparison test

Words: 58
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
If 0≤an​≤bn​ eventually and ∑bn​ converges, then ∑an​ converges. The nondecreasing partial sums of the nonnegative an​ are bounded above by a finite initial contribution plus the sum of bn​; bounded monotone sequence theorem proves the claim. Consequently ∣cn​∣≤bn​ with summable bn​ proves absolute convergence of ∑cn​. Finite changes to initial terms do not affect convergence.

Dyadic-block alternation of reciprocal terms (a2n+r​=(−1)n/(2n+r))

Words: 57
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
For 0≤r<2n and n≥0, the displayed sequence tends to zero, but its series diverges. The signed sum across the nth dyadic block has magnitude ∑r=02n−1​(2n+r)−1≥1/2. Differences of arbitrarily late partial sums therefore fail the Cauchy sequence condition on partial sums. Alternating signs between blocks do not rescue convergence when the total contribution of an entire block stays away from zero.

Lucas number (L0​=2, L1​=1, Ln+2​=Ln+1​+Ln​)

Words: 42
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
The Lucas numbers obey the same second-order recurrence as the Fibonacci numbers but start with 2,1, so their sequence is 2,1,3,4,7,11,…. For n≥1, Ln​=Fn−1​+Fn+1​. Substitution in the Fibonacci addition formula gives F2n​=Fn​Ln​. Consecutive Fibonacci numbers are coprime by the Euclidean algorithm; since Ln​=Fn​+2Fn−1​, Bézout's identity gives gcd(Fn​,Ln​)=gcd(Fn​,2)≤2.

Sequence ((xn​)n=1∞​)

Words: 4k Articles: 64
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
A sequence assigns a value to each position in an ordered index list. For an infinite sequence in a set X, one standard convention is a function x:N>0​→X, written (xn​)n=1∞​ with xn​=x(n). Some applications start the index at zero, and a finite sequence has only finitely many positions. Values may repeat; both order and repetition matter. [ref].
For example, an​=(−1)n begins −1,1,−1,1,…, whereas bn​=(−1)n+1 begins 1,−1,1,−1,…. Their sets of values are both {−1,1}, but these are different sequences. A subsequence keeps selected positions in increasing order; the subsequence of an​ at its even integers is the constant sequence 1,1,1,…. A tail of a sequence retains all positions from one index onward.
Sequences express successive approximations, repeated observations, and the iterates of a recurrence relation. A limit of a sequence describes where its terms eventually concentrate. Finite observations alone cannot establish that behaviour: for any positive integer K, the all-zero sequence and the sequence with un​=0 for n≤K and un​=1 for n>K agree through index K, yet have different limits of sequences. A formula or bound controlling the entire future, such as the tail diameter of a sequence in the Cauchy sequence condition, supplies information that a finite list cannot.

Kolakoski sequence

Words: 29
Sequence OurBigBook.com
A sequence equal to its own sequence of consecutive run lengths. The classical sequence uses the alphabet {1,2} and begins 1,2,2,1,1,2,1,2,2,…; variants use other pairs of positive integers.

Eventually periodic sequence (un+T​=un​(n≥N))

Words: 139 Articles: 1
Sequence OurBigBook.com
A sequence is eventually periodic if there are integers N≥0 and T>0 such that un+T​=un​ for all n≥N. It consists of a finite initial segment followed by a repeating period. Checking finitely many repeated values can suggest eventual periodicity, but a proof requires a reason the repetition continues, such as recurrence of a complete state in a deterministic finite-state process.

Sum of an eventually periodic sequence (∑j=0L−1​uN+j​=qC+∑j=0r−1​uN+j​,L=qT+r)

Words: 79
Eventually periodic sequence OurBigBook.com
Suppose a numerical sequence has period T from index N, and let C=∑j=0T−1​uN+j​. For L=qT+r with 0≤r<T, split the required sum into q complete periods and a tail of length r. Every complete period contributes C, proving the formula in the title. Precomputed prefix sums of one period make the tail lookup constant time. If this periodic sequence consists of the first differences of another sequence, the same formula extrapolates that original sequence by adding the initial value at N.

Look-and-say sequence

Words: 40
Sequence OurBigBook.com
Each term is obtained by reading the lengths and values of consecutive runs in the previous term. Starting from 1 gives 1,11,21,1211,111221,…: for example, 21 contains one 2 followed by one 1, so its successor is 1211.

Rudin-Shapiro sequence (b(n))

Words: 29
Sequence OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative integer n, let r(n) count overlapping occurrences of 11 in its binary expansion. The Rudin-Shapiro sign sequence is b(n)=(−1)r(n). Appending a binary digit gives b(2n)=b(n) and b(2n+1)=(−1)nb(n).

Beatty's theorem

Beatty sequence OurBigBook.com
If α,β>1 are irrational numbers with 1/α+1/β=1, the Beatty sequences ⌊nα⌋ and ⌊nβ⌋ partition the positive integers.

Fibonacci word

Words: 58
Sequence OurBigBook.com
A word formed recursively by concatenating the previous two words in a specified order, for example Wn​=Wn−2​Wn−1​ from two seed words. Lengths satisfy the Fibonacci recurrence. To locate a symbol, compare its index with the first block's length, choose the containing block, and subtract the first length when entering the second block. This avoids constructing an exponentially long word.

Elliptic divisibility sequence
Words: 36
Divisibility sequence OurBigBook.com
A divisibility sequence associated with multiples of a point on an elliptic curve, using suitably normalized division polynomials. With W0​=0 and W1​=1, its terms satisfy the Ward identity Wm+n​Wm−n​=Wm+1​Wm−1​Wn2​−Wn+1​Wn−1​Wm2​. Setting nearby indices gives doubling identities, enabling logarithmic-depth evaluation.

Ulam sequence

Words: 44
Integer sequence OurBigBook.com
Starting with two distinct positive integers a<b, repeatedly append the smallest integer larger than the previous term that is expressible in exactly one way as the sum of two distinct earlier terms. Requiring distinct summands and counting unordered pairs are both essential parts of the definition.

Golomb sequence (G(n))

Words: 31
Integer sequence OurBigBook.com
The nondecreasing sequence of positive integers beginning with G(1)=1 in which the integer n occurs exactly G(n) times. Its first terms are 1,2,2,3,3,4,4,4,5,5,5,…. The prefix sum ∑j=1k​G(j) gives the last position occupied by k.

Tribonacci number

Words: 38
Integer sequence OurBigBook.com
Terms of a sequence satisfying the third-order linear recurrence Tn+3​=Tn​+Tn+1​+Tn+2​. Initial values vary by convention; some counting problems specify T1​=T2​=T3​=1. To study divisibility by m, retain three consecutive remainders modulo m, a deterministic state with at most m3 possibilities.

Collatz sequence

Words: 40 Articles: 1
Sequence OurBigBook.com
For a positive integer a0​, define ak+1​=ak​/2 when ak​ is an even number, and ak+1​=3ak​+1 when ak​ is an odd number. Starting at 6 gives 6,3,10,5,16,8,4,2,1. Computing many trajectories benefits from memoization, since trajectories that reach the same value have identical continuations.

Periodic sequence (an+p​=an​)

Words: 34
Sequence OurBigBook.com
A sequence indexed from zero with an integer period p≥1 satisfying the displayed identity for all n≥0. Repeating a finite cycle is an example. The Cesàro mean article explains why its cumulative averages approach the one-cycle arithmetic mean.

Tail of a sequence ((xn​)n≥N​)

Words: 60
Sequence OurBigBook.com
A tail of a sequence consists of its terms from some index N onward, retaining their order and repetitions. Discarding finitely many initial terms does not change its limit of a sequence or whether it is a Cauchy sequence. A tail can also be considered as the set of values {xn​:n≥N} when forming an infimum, supremum, or tail diameter of a sequence; that set alone forgets the original order and repetitions.

Limit inferior and limit superior (liminf, limsup)

Words: 505 Articles: 1
Sequence OurBigBook.com
The limit inferior and limit superior retain the lower and upper long-run behaviour of a real sequence, even when it has no ordinary limit of a sequence. For each tail of a sequence beginning at N, define
lN​=inf{an​:n≥N},uN​=sup{an​:n≥N}.
(1)
Discarding more initial terms raises or preserves the infimum and lowers or preserves the supremum. Hence (lN​) is nondecreasing and (uN​) is nonincreasing. Their limits exist in the extended real number line:
liminfn→∞​an​=limN→∞​lN​=supN​lN​,limsupn→∞​an​=limN→∞​uN​=infN​uN​.
(2)
For a bounded sequence, both values are finite and liminfan​≤limsupan​. These bounds use the entire infinite tail of a sequence, rather than the last few observed terms. [ref].
Take the original example an​=(−1)n(1+1/n), beginning −2,3/2,−4/3,5/4,…. The subsequence at even integers decreases toward one, while the subsequence at odd integers increases toward minus one. If eN​ is the first even integer at least N and oN​ is the first odd integer at least N, then
uN​=1+1/eN​,lN​=−1−1/oN​.
(3)
Thus liminfan​=−1 and limsupan​=1. The finite initial extreme a1​=−2 disappears from later lower bounds; neither long-run value is attained by any term of this example.
For a bounded sequence, the limit inferior is the smallest subsequential limit and the limit superior is the largest subsequential limit; both are reached by suitable convergent subsequences. Every other subsequential limit lies between them. In the example there are only two subsequential limits, −1 and 1: a convergent subsequence cannot retain infinitely many terms of both parities, because those two branches stay separated. The whole interval between the two bounds need not consist of subsequential limits. [ref].
A finite ordinary limit of a sequence exists exactly when the limit inferior and limit superior agree at the same finite value L. The bounds lN​≤aN​≤uN​ and the squeeze theorem prove the sufficient direction. For a bounded sequence, its tail diameter of a sequence is DN​=uN​−lN​, so the limiting gap is zero exactly when the Cauchy sequence condition holds. In the example the gap approaches two, not zero. The same framework allows infinite bounds: an​=n has both values +∞, whereas an​=(−1)nn has limit inferior −∞ and limit superior +∞. Equality at infinity describes escape rather than convergence to a real value. [ref].

Limit inferior (liminf)

Words: 116
Limit inferior and limit superior OurBigBook.com
The limit inferior of a real sequence is
liminfn→∞​an​=supN​infn≥N​an​,
(4)
allowing a value in the extended real number line. For a finite value L, it has two complementary meanings: for every ε>0, all sufficiently late terms satisfy an​>L−ε, while arbitrarily late terms satisfy an​<L+ε. The first prevents persistent dips below L; the second prevents any larger number from being the true lower edge.
For an​=(−1)n(1+1/n), the lower bounds in limit inferior and limit superior approach −1. Every late term eventually exceeds −1−ε, and the subsequence at odd integers comes arbitrarily close to −1. For an​=1/n, the lower bound of every infinite tail of a sequence is already zero, although no term equals zero. Thus a limit inferior need not be the minimum of any tail.

Recurrence relation

Words: 115 Articles: 3
Sequence OurBigBook.com
A recurrence relation specifies members of a sequence in terms of previous members, together with enough initial values to determine the sequence. A three-term recurrence for orthogonal polynomials relates consecutive orders. For example, the physicists' Hermite polynomials satisfy Hn+1​(x)=2xHn​(x)−2nHn−1​(x), starting from H0​=1 and H1​=2x.

Recurrence relation OurBigBook.com
A linear recurrence ∑j=0r​pj​(n)an+j​=0 whose coefficients pj​(n) are polynomials in the index. A sequence satisfying such a relation is P-recursive.

Difference equation (zn+1​=F(zn​))

Words: 56
Recurrence relation OurBigBook.com
A difference equation relates values of a sequence at different indices, or its finite differences. A first-order autonomous system has the displayed form, with a scalar or vector state. Writing zn+1​−zn​=F(zn​)−zn​ gives its equivalent finite-difference form. Its fixed point stability is determined by the Jacobian matrix of the update and the unit circle, whereas a continuous-time differential equation uses the real parts of its linearized eigenvalues.

Thue–Morse sequence (tn​=s2​(n)mod2)

Words: 181 Articles: 3
Sequence OurBigBook.com
Here s2​(n) is the sum of the binary digits of the nonnegative integer n. The sign version is f(n)=(−1)s2​(n). Concatenating binary digits gives f(a2j+r)=f(a)f(r) for 0≤r<2j. It supplies cancellation controlled by binary blocks rather than multiplicative factorization.

Thue–Morse Fourier product (∑r<2j​(−1)s2​(r)e(rθ)=∏l=0j−1​(1−e(2lθ)))

Words: 143 Articles: 2
Thue–Morse sequence OurBigBook.com
Each binary digit independently contributes either 1 or −e(2lθ), proving the product. Two adjacent factors have modulus 8∣cos(πt)∣(1−cos2(πt))≤16/(33​)<4. Consequently the product is O(2σj), with σ=2−43​log2​3<1. This two-factor estimate suffices for a power saving, though its exponent is not optimal.
Uniform interval cancellation for binary digit parity (supJ⊂[0,N],θ​∣∑n∈J​(−1)s2​(n)e(nθ)∣≪Nσ)
Words: 98 Articles: 1
Thue–Morse Fourier product OurBigBook.com
An integer interval is a disjoint union of aligned binary blocks with at most two of each length. On [a2j,(a+1)2j) the Thue–Morse sequence sign factors as f(a)f(r), so the Thue–Morse Fourier product bounds its exponential sum by O(2σj). Sum the geometric series over block lengths to obtain the uniform bound, for σ=2−43​log2​3.
Small Type I sums for binary digit parity (N−1∑m≤N1/100​∣∑n∈Im​​(−1)s2​(mn)∣≪Nσ+1/100−1)
Words: 48
Uniform interval cancellation for binary digit parity OurBigBook.com
The additive character orthogonality filter 1m∣r​=m−1∑a=0m−1​e(ar/m) restricts the uniform interval cancellation for binary digit parity to multiples of m, without increasing its bound. Each inner Type I sum is therefore O(Nσ). Summing the at most N1/100 outer terms proves the displayed estimate, which is smaller than every fixed negative power of logN for large N.

Cluster-set matching of bounded sequences (∣amk​​−bnk​​∣⟶0)

Words: 105
Sequence OurBigBook.com
Two bounded real sequences with the same set of subsequential limits admit permutations that match their terms with differences tending to zero. Alternate between taking the least unused index of the first sequence and of the second. Match its value to an unused term of the other sequence near a nearest common cluster point, with additional error at most 1/j at stage j. Every cluster-point neighbourhood contains infinitely many available terms. The actively chosen indices tend to infinity, whose distance to the common cluster set tends to zero by boundedness. By step 2j, both lists have included every index up to j.

Fejér monotonicity (∥zk+1−p∥≤∥zk−p∥)

Words: 52
Sequence OurBigBook.com
A sequence is Fejér monotone with respect to a nonempty set C if ∥zk+1−p∥≤∥zk−p∥ for every p∈C. It is bounded. If it has a cluster point zˉ∈C, its nonincreasing distance to zˉ and that convergent subsequence force the entire sequence to converge to zˉ.

Finite repetition-free sequence (Inj(<ω,X))

Words: 57
Sequence OurBigBook.com
A finite repetition-free sequence in a set X is an injective function from an initial segment {0,…,k−1} of the natural numbers into X, including the empty sequence for k=0. For a finite set of size m, the number of these sequences is
∑k=0m​(m−k)!m!​.
(5)
The order of each list is part of the data, so it can be enumerated without choosing an order on its underlying support.

Geometric progression (an​=arn)

Words: 252 Articles: 1
Sequence OurBigBook.com
A geometric progression is a sequence obtained by repeatedly multiplying by one fixed common ratio r:
a0​=a,an+1​=ran​,an​=arn(n≥0).
(7)
Here a and r may be real numbers or complex numbers. The recurrence is meaningful even when a=0 or r=0; expressing r as a ratio of successive terms requires a nonzero denominator. As a polynomial convention, r0=1, including at r=0.
For example, quantities 100,80,64,51.2,… retain four fifths of their preceding value at every step. The decrement changes, but the retained fraction does not. With the same initial value and common ratio 2, the terms are 100,200,400,800,…. This multiplicative structure is useful whenever the same proportional rule repeats: it turns many updates into the single exponentiation rn. An arithmetic progression instead repeats an additive increment.
For nonzero a, the modulus of an​ tends to zero when ∣r∣<1, stays fixed when ∣r∣=1, and grows without bound when ∣r∣>1. For a negative real common ratio, successive nonzero terms also alternate in sign. Thus the terms 1,−1/2,1/4,−1/8,… decay in size while crossing zero at every step. Adding the terms gives a geometric series; the individual terms and their accumulated partial sums are different sequences.

Geometric progression OurBigBook.com
The common ratio of a geometric progression is the multiplier r in an+1​=ran​. Whenever an​=0, it can be recovered as an+1​/an​. For a=0 and r=0, the first step gives zero and all subsequent terms remain zero, so those later quotients are undefined even though the recurrence remains valid. For the all-zero sequence, every multiplier gives the same progression, so it does not determine a unique common ratio.

Subsequential limit (ank​​→L)

Words: 97
Subsequence OurBigBook.com
A subsequential limit of a sequence (an​) is a value L approached by some subsequence (ank​​) with strictly increasing indices nk​. For an​=(−1)n(1+1/n), the subsequences at even integers and odd integers give subsequential limits one and minus one. A finite value appearing among only finitely many initial terms does not become a subsequential limit merely by being a member of the image of a function represented by the sequence.
For a bounded sequence of real numbers, its subsequential limits form a nonempty bounded set that is also a closed set. The Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem guarantees nonemptiness, and its extreme values are the limit inferior and limit superior. The sequence in sparse peaks can determine a limit superior has the two subsequential limits zero and one, despite almost all indices in the natural density sense carrying zero.

Monotone subsequence theorem

Subsequence OurBigBook.com
Every real sequence has a monotone subsequence, without a boundedness assumption. Call an index a peak when its term is at least every later term. Infinitely many peaks give a nonincreasing subsequence; beyond finitely many peaks each term has a larger later term, which recursively gives an increasing subsequence.

Uncountability by interleaving prescribed binary coordinates

Words: 78
Bitstream OurBigBook.com
Partition the positive natural numbers into three infinite coordinate sets. Fix the coordinates on the first two sets to any prescribed binary values, and leave those on the third set free. Reading the third coordinate set embeds all infinite binary sequences in the resulting family, so the family is an uncountable set by Cantor's diagonal argument. For example, fixing x3k−2​=0 and x3k−1​=a3k−1​ while leaving x3k​ free guarantees infinitely many zeros and infinitely many agreements with any prescribed binary sequence (an​). Infinite free coordinates remain even after both requirements are enforced.

Monotone sequence

Words: 2k Articles: 9
Sequence OurBigBook.com
A real sequence is increasing when an+1​≥an​ and decreasing when an+1​≤an​.
A monotone sequence has one of these directions for every index. Here increasing means nondecreasing and decreasing means nonincreasing: equal successive terms are allowed. Strict increase would require an+1​>an​ at every step, and strict decrease would require an+1​<an​. A constant sequence is both increasing and decreasing. These conventions are those of Basic Analysis: Introduction to Real Analysis, Volume I by Jiří Lebl (§2.1.1, Definition 2.1.9).
For n≥1, the sequence 1−1/n increases toward one, while 1+1/n decreases toward one. Repeating each term gives the still increasing sequence 0,0,1/2,1/2,2/3,2/3,…. Plateaus do not obstruct the bounded monotone sequence theorem. Checking the sign of an+1​−an​ is often the simplest way to verify a direction; finding an upper bound or lower bound is a separate task.

Bounded monotone sequence theorem

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Monotone sequence OurBigBook.com
A monotone sequence of real numbers has a finite limit of a sequence exactly when it is a bounded sequence. In the increasing case, only an upper bound needs to be supplied, because the first term already gives a lower bound; in the decreasing case, only a lower bound needs to be supplied. The limit of a sequence is the exact edge of the set of terms:
an​≤an+1​≤M⟹an​⟶L=sup{an​:n≥1},
(8)
m≤bn+1​≤bn​⟹bn​⟶L=inf{bn​:n≥1}.
(9)
The upper bound M or lower bound m need not itself be the limit of a sequence. A supremum or infimum identifies the sharp bound. [ref]
For example, an​=1−1/n is increasing and bounded above by one, and bn​=1+1/n is decreasing and bounded below by one. Both have limit of a sequence one, although neither ever equals one. Their absolute errors are exactly 1/n. They also bracket any sequence xn​ satisfying an​≤xn​≤bn​: the squeeze theorem gives xn​→1, even if (xn​) itself is not a monotone sequence.
The theorem is useful when a recurrence relation gives successive improvements and a bound, before the answer has been identified. It proves existence of a limit of a sequence; further algebra, often using continuity, identifies the answer. A finite plot illustrates the formulas but does not establish the infinite claim. Error bounds for bounded monotone sequences require additional quantitative information.
A real increasing sequence bounded above converges to its supremum; a decreasing sequence bounded below converges to its infimum. For the increasing case, the definition of supremum provides a term above L−ε, and every later term remains between that term and L. Negation reduces the decreasing case to the increasing case. This elementary result is distinct from the measure-theoretic monotone convergence theorem for integrals.
The existence of the real supremum in this short proof uses the least-upper-bound property, equivalently completeness of the real numbers. The approximation property of a supremum supplies aN​>L−ε, and monotonicity keeps every later term within the same tolerance:
n≥N⟹0≤L−an​≤L−aN​<ε.
(10)
The corresponding decreasing statement follows from the approximation property of an infimum. The converse uses the fact that every convergent sequence is a bounded sequence. [ref]

The supremum of an increasing bounded sequence need not be a maximum of its set of terms. Dropping either condition destroys the implication. The increasing sequence an​=n has a lower bound one but no upper bound, and no finite limit of a sequence. Its subsequence at even integers is constantly one, and its subsequence at odd integers is constantly minus one. These two subsequential limits cannot both equal a single limit of a sequence. [ref]

qn​=2n⌊2n2​⌋​,n≥1.

Bounded monotone sequence theorem OurBigBook.com
For an increasing sequence converging to L, its absolute error is en​=L−an​≥0 and is nonincreasing. For a decreasing sequence, the absolute error is en​=an​−L≥0 and is also nonincreasing. This tells us that later terms cannot be worse, but does not supply a computable stopping index for a chosen tolerance.
Suppose an increasing lower approximation an​ and a decreasing upper approximation bn​ enclose the same limit of a sequence L. Their observable gap wn​=bn​−an​ gives
an​≤L≤bn​⟹∣an​−L∣≤wn​,∣bn​−L∣≤wn​,​2an​+bn​​−L​≤2wn​​.

The bound is valid even when such symmetry is absent.

an​={0,1−2−(n−K),​n≤K,n>K.​

This is an increasing bounded sequence converging to one, but its absolute error is one through index K. Since K can exceed any proposed index, the bounded monotone sequence theorem alone cannot say when the absolute error will fall below 1/2. A zero difference between two successive terms is also insufficient: the initial plateau eventually ends.
There is no universal eventual rate either. Let (rn​) be any proposed positive nonincreasing sequence tending to zero, with rn​≤1. Set
an​=1−rn​​.

Indeed, rn​​/rn​=1/rn​​→∞, so no fixed constant multiple of rn​ bounds the absolute error eventually. If a proposed rate is not nonincreasing, replace it, after a finite initial segment if necessary, by the decreasing envelope sn​=sup{rk​:k≥n}; this also tends to zero, and the same construction defeats the original rate. Series (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
A double series is a series whose terms carry two indices. For nonnegative terms, define its sum as the supremum of all finite subsums; iterated sums in either order give this same value, possibly infinity. For absolutely summable terms, both orders also agree and give a finite sum. Without these hypotheses, an order of summation must be specified and changing it can change the result. A triangular index set, such as 0≤n≤m, can be represented by setting the other terms to zero.

Cesàro summation (σN​=(N+1)−1∑n=0N​sn​)

Words: 717 Articles: 6
Summation method OurBigBook.com
Cesàro summation assigns a value to a series when the arithmetic means of its partial sums approach a finite limit of a sequence. Here we use the first-order method, often written (C,1). For a real or complex series beginning at index zero, define
sn​=∑k=0n​ak​,σN​=N+11​∑n=0N​sn​.
(20)
It is Cesàro summable to L when σN​→L. The averaging is applied to the partial sums sn​, rather than to the original terms an​. This distinction is essential: the terms can average to zero while their accumulated sum keeps growing. [ref]
For Grandi's series 1−1+1−1+⋯, the partial sums alternate between one and zero. The series is not a convergent series, but the two values occupy asymptotically equal proportions of the averaging window. In the declared index convention,
σ2m​=2m+1m+1​,σ2m+1​=21​,
(21)
so its first-order Cesàro sum is 1/2. This names a particular summation method; it does not turn the oscillating partial sums into an ordinarily convergent sequence.
Why is this useful? An oscillating approximation can retain stable information when its cumulative average settles. Because the Cesàro theorem for convergent sequences preserves an existing limit of a sequence, this adds some new cases without changing the sum of any ordinarily convergent series. For Fourier series, averaging the Fourier partial sums gives a Fejér sum; the existing Fejér kernel and approximation articles explain its effect on reconstruction. Averaging does not guarantee success for every oscillating sequence, as the bounded partial sums need not be Cesàro summable example shows.
One historical motivation was the multiplication of series. In 1918, A. F. Andersen recalled Ernesto Cesàro's product theorem and cited his 1890 publication at the start of a study of products involving Cesàro summable series. This connects the theory with preserving useful operations on sums, as well as with assigning a value to an isolated example. His paper treats several orders of summability; the examples here use only (C,1).[ref]

Telescoping series (∑n=1N​(bn​−bn+1​)=b1​−bN+1​)

Words: 280 Articles: 1
Series (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
A telescoping series has partial sums in which internal contributions cancel. The basic pattern is an​=bn​−bn+1​, for which finite summation gives
∑n=1N​(bn​−bn+1​)=(b1​−b2​)+(b2​−b3​)+⋯+(bN​−bN+1​)=b1​−bN+1​.
(26)
Only the two boundary terms survive. If bn​ tends to a finite limit of a sequence L, the series consequently sums to b1​−L. The cancellation is exact for each finite N; the infinite result then follows by a limit of a sequence.
For example, partial fraction decomposition gives
n(n+1)1​=n1​−n+11​,∑n=1N​n(n+1)1​=1−N+11​.
(27)
The first three terms are 1/2,1/6,1/12, with partial sum 3/4. The first five have partial sum 5/6. Taking the limit of a sequence gives the concise answer
n=1∑∞​n(n+1)1​=1​.
(28)
The appeal is that a long calculation becomes a boundary calculation. It works whenever the summand is a successive difference, not only for rational functions. For instance, an​=log((n+1)/n)=log(n+1)−logn gives partial sum log(N+1), so its series diverges despite the cancellation. A telescoping series therefore need not be a convergent series: one must still examine the surviving boundary term.

Tail of a telescoping reciprocal series (∑n=N+1∞​n(n+1)1​=N+11​)

Words: 100
Telescoping series OurBigBook.com
For the telescoping series ∑n=1∞​1/[n(n+1)]=1, the remainder after the first N terms is exactly
1−SN​=∑n=N+1∞​n(n+1)1​=N+11​.
(29)
Thus S9​=0.9, S99​=0.99, and S999​=0.999. This supplies an exact stopping rule: to make the absolute error at most 10−3, 999 terms suffice. Requiring strictly less than 10−3 instead needs at least 1000 terms.
The next term, aN+1​=1/[(N+1)(N+2)], is smaller than the full remaining sum by a factor of N+2. For example, after 99 terms the next term is 1/10100, while the remainder is 1/100. The term test for divergence concerns individual terms; a reliable numerical approximation needs a bound on the whole remaining sum.

Term test for divergence

Words: 86
Series (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
The term test for divergence says that a series cannot converge if its terms fail to tend to zero. Indeed, if its partial sums satisfy Sn​→S, then an​=Sn​−Sn−1​→S−S=0. This is a necessary condition for a convergent series.
The converse fails: 1/n→0, but the harmonic series diverges. For a quick successful test, ∑n=1∞​n/(n+1) diverges because its terms tend to one. The test gives no conclusion for ∑1/n or ∑1/[n(n+1)]: both have terms tending to zero, yet only the second is a convergent series. The telescoping series calculation and the harmonic series block estimate resolve those cases.

If a tail of holomorphic factors admits logarithms whose absolute values have a summable bound uniformly on every compact set, their product converges locally uniformly to the exponential of the logarithmic sum. The tail is holomorphic and nowhere zero. Finite initial factors may have zeros; those finite factors determine the locations and orders of all zeros near any given compact set. The scalar sufficient condition ∑j​∣uj​∣<∞ for factors 1+uj​ follows from ∣log(1+uj​)∣≤2∣uj​∣ for ∣uj​∣≤1/2.

Harmonic series (∑n=1∞​n1​)

Words: 441 Articles: 1
Series (mathematics) OurBigBook.com
The harmonic series is the positive series
1+21​+31​+41​+⋯=∑n=1∞​n1​.
(33)
Its partial sums are the harmonic numbers HN​. Although the individual terms tend to zero, HN​ grows without bound, so the harmonic series is not a convergent series. This is a basic warning against using the size of one term as a bound on all the terms still to come.
The growth is slow enough to be visually deceptive. The partial sums at N=10,100,1000,10000 are approximately 2.92896825,5.18737752,7.48547086,9.78760604. Adding ten times as many terms increases the accumulated total by roughly log10≈2.30258509, rather than multiplying the total by ten. The telescoping series ∑1/[n(n+1)] has similarly vanishing terms but approaches the finite sum one.
A short block argument proves the divergence without trusting a finite plot. For each integer k≥0, the block from 2k+1 through 2k+1 contains 2k terms, each at least 1/2k+1. Therefore
∑n=2k+12k+1​n1​≥21​,H2m​≥1+2m​.
(34)
Every doubling supplies at least another half, and arbitrarily many doublings are possible. A collection of tiny terms can still have a substantial combined contribution. See Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis I, Example 2.5.11 for this grouping proof.
Integral comparison sharpens the growth estimate. Here log denotes the natural logarithm. Since 1/x is a strictly decreasing function for positive x, comparison of rectangles with the integral gives
log(N+1)≤HN​≤1+logN.
(35)
Thus the divergence is logarithmic. The finer difference HN​−logN tends to the Euler--Mascheroni constant, approximately 0.57721566; the harmonic number expansion supplies higher-order corrections. This turns the counterexample into a usable quantitative estimate of accumulated reciprocal contributions.
Euler's De progressionibus harmonicis observationes, written in 1734 and published in 1740, studies these sums beyond the yes-or-no question of convergence. Sections 2–3 compare long blocks to show continued growth, and later sections compare the sums with logarithms and calculate the constant offset. The [ref] identifies the dates and original publication; [ref] makes the calculations accessible. This is not a claim that Euler first discovered divergence: the paper's interest includes measuring how slowly a divergent sum grows.

Words: 63
Harmonic series OurBigBook.com
The alternating harmonic series ∑n≥1​(−1)n+1/n converges. Its even partial sums increase, its odd partial sums decrease, and the two limits agree because their difference is the next term. In particular, every even partial sum is a lower bound and every odd partial sum is an upper bound for the limit.
This alternates the signs of the terms of the harmonic series, which itself diverges.

For a real subadditive sequence (xn​)n≥1​, the normalized sequence has the extended-real limit of a sequence

No lower-bound hypothesis is needed for this conclusion. The limit of a sequence is finite precisely when the ratios are bounded below. The example xn​=−n2 is a subadditive sequence with normalized limit of a sequence −∞.
To prove the result, fix k≥1 and, for n≥k, write n=qk+r with q≥1 and 0≤r<k. Iterating subadditivity gives xn​≤qxk​+Ck​, where Ck​=max(0,x1​,…,xk−1​) and C1​=0. Hence limsupn​xn​/n≤xk​/k for every k. Every ratio is at least their infimum. If that infimum is finite these bounds identify the limit of a sequence; if it is −∞, choosing k with an arbitrarily negative ratio gives convergence to −∞.

Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem (xnj​​→ℓ)

Words: 716 Articles: 6
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
Every bounded sequence of real numbers contains a subsequence with a finite limit of a sequence. If ∣xn​∣≤M for every positive integer n, there are integers n1​<n2​<⋯ and a real number ℓ such that
limj→∞​xnj​​=ℓ.
(37)
The increasing indices matter: a subsequence retains the original order and selects terms arbitrarily far along the original sequence. The theorem guarantees the existence of at least one such selection; it does not claim that the entire sequence converges or that the subsequential limit is unique.[ref]
For example, the bounded sequence xn​=(−1)n+1/(n+1) has two distinct subsequential limits:
x2j​=1+2j+11​⟶1,x2j−1​=−1+2j1​⟶−1.
(38)
The even terms form a convergent sequence, and so do the odd terms. The full sequence cannot have a limit of a sequence because its two subsequences have different limits. Its limit superior is 1 and its limit inferior is −1.
This is useful when a construction produces many candidate points but does not immediately produce a convergent sequence. For a continuous function on a nonempty closed bounded feasible region in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, take a sequence whose objective values approach the infimum. A convergent subsequence supplies a candidate point; a closed subset retains that point, and continuity passes the objective values to the limit of a sequence. This is the mechanism behind attainment in the extreme value theorem. The diagonal subsequence argument extends the real-sequence theorem to finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
The theorem is named for Bernard Bolzano and Karl Weierstrass.[ref]

At least one of the two closed halves contains infinitely many indexed terms; choose such a half and repeat. This gives nested intervals Ij​ with lengths (b−a)/2j. The nested interval theorem, using completeness of the real numbers, supplies their unique common point ℓ.
Choose nj​>nj−1​ with xnj​​∈Ij​. Infinitely many indexed terms in Ij​ guarantee that the next index can be chosen. Both xnj​​ and ℓ belong to Ij​, so
∣xnj​​−ℓ∣≤2jb−a​⟶0.

Boundedness alone therefore does not give the corresponding theorem in every metric space; completeness of the real numbers is doing real work here. The floor function simply truncates the decimal expansion in this example.

In the l2 sequence space, let en​ have value one in coordinate n and zero elsewhere. This orthonormal sequence is bounded: ∥en​∥2​=1. For distinct indices n,m, its terms obey ∥en​−em​∥2​=2​. No subsequence can therefore be a Cauchy sequence, so none converges in the norm. Thus even a complete metric space can have a bounded sequence with no convergent subsequence. Finite dimension is essential to the usual Euclidean space extension, and in a general metric space the relevant replacement is compactness or total boundedness together with completeness.

Limit of a sequence (limn→∞​xn​)

Words: 263 Articles: 1
Convergent sequence OurBigBook.com
A sequence (xn​)n≥1​ of real numbers has limit of a sequence L∈R, written xn​→L, precisely when
∀ε>0∃N∈N>0​∀n≥N:∣xn​−L∣<ε.
(40)
The absolute value measures the error. The tolerance ε is chosen first; N may depend on it, but must control every later term. Infinitely many accurate terms alone do not suffice. For example, xn​=(−1)n repeatedly equals one but also repeatedly differs from one by two. The definition and uniqueness of the limit of a sequence are discussed in MIT 18.100A, Lecture 6, definitions 13 and theorem 15.
For a worked error estimate, let xn​=3+2/n. Then ∣xn​−3∣=2/n, so any positive integer N>2/ε works. With ε=0.01, choose N=201; every later error is at most 2/201<0.01. The strict inequality matters: N=200 would give equality at its first term. A limit of a sequence turns the informal instruction “take enough terms” into an explicit accuracy guarantee.
The limit of a sequence is unique: two distinct proposed answers cannot both be within arbitrarily small error of every late term, by the triangle inequality. Changing finitely many initial terms does not change it. For an extended real number, xn​→+∞ means ∀M∈R∃N∀n≥N: xn​>M; convergence to −∞ similarly requires xn​<M. These describe escape rather than a finite answer. The extended-real Fekete lemma is an example where the limit of a sequence need not be finite.

Cesàro mean (n1​∑k=1n​ak​)

Words: 211 Articles: 1
Convergent sequence OurBigBook.com
The Cesàro mean of the first n≥1 terms of a sequence is their arithmetic mean. It is a cumulative average: increasing n includes the whole initial segment, rather than a fixed-length sliding window. For ak​=(−1)k, the even-length averages are zero and the odd-length averages are −1/n, so they tend to zero even though the sequence does not converge.
For a periodic sequence with period p≥1 and one-cycle arithmetic mean M, split an initial segment into full cycles and a remainder of fewer than p terms. The full cycles contribute exactly M per term; the remainder contributes a fixed bounded error divided by n. Thus the Cesàro means tend to M. The cycle 0,2,1 in the bounded partial sums need not be Cesàro summable illustration has arithmetic mean one. Treating it as a sequence of partial sums gives a series with first-order Cesàro sum one; averaging a sequence and summing its terms remain different operations.

At x=0 and x=1, the error from this pointwise limit is already zero, so N=1 works. Nevertheless, N(x,ε) grows without bound as x→1 from below. A finite list of accurate test inputs cannot establish uniform convergence.
An even sharper warning concerns integration. On [0,1], define the continuous functions
gn​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​2n2x,2n−2n2x,0,​0≤x≤1/(2n),1/(2n)≤x≤1/n,1/n≤x≤1.​
(47)
Their supports are [0,1/n], with height n at 1/(2n) and value zero at both ends. Every fixed x>0 eventually lies beyond the support, and gn​(0)=0 always, so pointwise convergence gives the zero function. Nevertheless, each integral is the area of a triangle: ∫01​gn​(x)dx=21​(1/n)n=21​. Shrinking width compensates increasing height. Hence the limit of a sequence of these integrals differs from the integral of the pointwise limit; interchanging them requires additional conditions, such as uniform convergence preserves integrals on a compact interval.

For fixed m, the inner limit is one precisely when m!x is an integer, and zero otherwise, because ∣cos(πy)∣=1 exactly at integers and powers of a number with modulus below one tend to zero. If x=p/q is a rational number, q divides m! for every m≥q, making the inner limit eventually one. If x is an irrational number, multiplication by a nonzero integer cannot make it integral, making every inner limit zero. The order of the two limits is essential to this argument.

They converge pointwise to zero and their integrals converge to zero, but their convergence is not uniform convergence. Thus convergence of integrals and continuity of the pointwise limit do not imply uniform convergence.

A pointwise limit assigns to each input the limit of a sequence of function values there, on the specified domain of a function. It is unique wherever it exists, by uniqueness of the numerical limit of a sequence. Its existence supplies no common approximation rate over the domain of a function. For fn​(x)=xn on [0,1], it equals zero below one and one at one; restricting to [0,a] with a<1 gives the zero function.

Power series (∑n=0∞​an​(z−c)n)

Words: 3k Articles: 33
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
A power series combines a sequence of coefficients with monomials in the displacement from a fixed centre:
∑n=0∞​an​(z−c)n.
(48)
The variable z, centre c, and coefficients can be real numbers or complex numbers. Its degree-N partial sum PN​(z)=∑n=0N​an​(z−c)n is a polynomial, so a convergent power series can turn a complicated function into increasingly accurate finite calculations. Convergence, and the error after stopping, are essential parts of that claim.
The geometric series supplies the simplest computed example:
1−z1​=1+z+z2+⋯,∣z∣<1.
(49)
At z=1/2, stopping after degree ten gives P10​(1/2)=1.9990234375, differing from the exact value 2 by 1/1024=0.0009765625. At z=0.99, the same degree gives only about 10.4662 instead of 100. The same formula has very different practical accuracy at different points; the geometric power-series remainder quantifies it.
The structure is useful beyond numerical evaluation. Within its radius of convergence, termwise differentiation of a power series turns a question about a derivative into a question about coefficients. A Taylor series chooses an​=f(n)(c)/n! when it represents the function locally. A formal power series instead uses the coefficients algebraically, without asserting numerical convergence; the existing generating function examples use that distinction to encode counting problems.

f(x)1​=a0​1​−a02​a1​​x+a03​a12​−a0​a2​​x2+O(x3).

[xn]g(x)m=∑j1​+⋯+jm​=nj1​,…,jm​≥1​​gj1​​⋯gjm​​.

Analyticity

Words: 61
Power series OurBigBook.com
Analyticity at a point means that a function agrees in a neighbourhood of that point with a convergent power series. This is stronger than merely having derivatives of every order: the Taylor series of a smooth function can fail to recover its values. For a real variable this property defines a real analytic function. For a complex variable it is equivalent to being a holomorphic function on a neighbourhood of the point.

Geometric power-series remainder (1−z1​−∑n=0N​zn=1−zzN+1​)

Power series OurBigBook.com
For the degree-N partial sum PN​(z)=1+z+⋯+zN of the geometric series, the finite identity (1−z)PN​(z)=1−zN+1 gives
1−z1​−PN​(z)=1−zzN+1​,z=1.
(52)
For any fixed 0<r<1, the triangle inequality then gives the uniform error bound
sup∣z∣≤r​​1−z1​−PN​(z)​≤1−rrN+1​.
(53)
Equality is attained at the positive real point z=r, so this is the exact worst-case error on that closed disk. It also proves uniform convergence on each such disk, not just pointwise convergence.
Given a positive tolerance ε, choosing N with rN+1/(1−r)≤ε turns a convergence statement into a finite stopping rule. For ε=10−3, degree ten suffices throughout ∣z∣≤1/2. Nearer the boundary, r=0.9 requires degree 87 and r=0.99 requires degree 1145. The required degree depends on both the tolerance and the region, not just on the name of the function.

Generating function (A(x)=∑n≥0​an​xn)

Words: 996 Articles: 6
Power series OurBigBook.com
A generating function packages a sequence into a series so that operations on objects become operations on their encodings. An ordinary generating function uses the power series A(z)=∑n≥0​an​zn; in counting problems, the coefficient an​ records the number of objects of size n. The variable z initially marks size: it need not be assigned a numerical value. Coefficient extraction writes this recovery as [zn]A(z)=an​. One compact expression can therefore answer infinitely many counting questions, while explaining how their answers fit together.
Start with two contributions: choose i from {0,1,2} and j from {0,1}, with exactly one option at each allowed value. Their individual ordinary generating functions are the polynomials P(x)=1+x+x2 and Q(x)=1+x. To count ordered pairs by total i+j, multiply:
P(x)Q(x)=(1+x+x2)(1+x)=1+2x+2x2+x3.
(54)
The coefficients 1,2,2,1 count the ways to obtain totals zero through three. For total two, the possibilities are (1,1) and (2,0); the two corresponding monomials both contribute x2. There are six ordered pairs altogether, agreeing with P(1)Q(1)=3⋅2=6.
If the first contribution has two distinguishable choices when i=1, replace P(x) by 1+2x+x2. Its product with Q(x) becomes 1+3x+3x2+x3. The coefficients now carry multiplicities as well as possible totals; the exponent still records cost. This lets the same construction handle several actions with identical costs without losing their separate identities.
In general, the Cauchy product gives
[zn](A(z)B(z))=∑k=0n​ak​bn−k​.
(55)
For each split of the total size, the rule of product counts the choices of the two components; summing over those splits counts all possibilities. This requires each combined object to have a unique decomposition into the two components. The same idea works for costs, lengths, or other additive measures, not just the number of pieces. See MIT 18.310, generating functions, sections 1–2.
Now cover a board of length n with tiles of lengths one and two, without gaps or overlaps. Let tn​ count these tilings. There is exactly one empty tiling, so t0​=1, and t1​=1. Removing the first tile leaves a board shorter by one or two, giving the recurrence relation
tn​=tn−1​+tn−2​(n≥2),(t0​,t1​,t2​,t3​,t4​,t5​)=(1,1,2,3,5,8).
(56)
These are the Fibonacci numbers shifted by one index: tn​=Fn+1​ under the convention F0​=0, F1​=1. Keeping the empty tiling is essential to both the counting rule and the resulting ordinary generating function.
For F(z)=∑n≥0​tn​zn, the empty board or a first tile followed by a remaining tiling gives
F(z)=1+(z+z2)F(z),F(z)=1−z−z21​=1+z+2z2+3z3+5z4+8z5+⋯.
(57)
Equivalently, F(z)=∑m≥0​(z+z2)m: each factor chooses one tile, and m counts pieces while the exponent of z records total length. The same ordinary generating function counts ordered histories of two repeatable actions costing one and two units. Histories (1,2) and (2,1) differ despite having the same total cost. MIT's notes use dots and dashes with these costs, including the empty message. [ref]
These identities hold in formal power series algebra: each requested coefficient uses only finitely many contributions. The repeated-choice expansion is legitimate because z+z2 has zero constant term; a zero-cost repeatable action would allow infinitely many histories of the same size. Numerical evaluation separately requires a convergent series. Here the radius of convergence is (5​−1)/2, the reciprocal of the golden ratio. At z=1, the rational function equals −1, but the counting series diverges: that value cannot represent its sum.
Other generating functions change the encoding: an exponential generating function divides by factorials, while a Dirichlet series uses n−s. A counting generating function also differs from a probability generating function, whose coefficients must be nonnegative and sum to one.

Exponential generating function (A(z)=∑n≥0​an​zn/n!)

Words: 313 Articles: 1
Generating function OurBigBook.com
An exponential generating function encodes a sequence using A(z)=∑n≥0​an​zn/n!. For labelled counting, an​ is the number of structures on a fixed set of n distinct labels. Labels distinguish otherwise similar objects: changing which person belongs to a group can change the structure. Recover the count by coefficient extraction as an​=n![zn]A(z). The raw coefficient is an​/n!, not an​.
The factorial makes multiplication account automatically for distributing labels. To combine an A-structure on k labels and a B-structure on the remaining n−k, choose the first label subset in (kn​) ways, then choose the two structures. The binomial coefficient counts how the two groups of labels interleave within the full label set. Thus
A(z)B(z)=∑n≥0​cn​n!zn​,cn​=∑k=0n​(kn​)ak​bn−k​.
(58)
The normalization works because 1/(k!(n−k)!)=(kn​)/n!. This explains the usefulness of exponential generating functions for labelled counting: an ordinary Cauchy product would omit the choices of labels. See Peter Magyar, Math 482, notes for 2/7, labelled product principle.
For a concrete example, there is one undecorated set on any given collection of labels. Its exponential generating function is the exponential function E(z)=ez=∑n≥0​zn/n!. Combine a red set and a blue set, allowing either to be empty:
E(z)E(z)=e2z=∑n≥0​2nn!zn​.
(59)
Every label independently receives one of two colours, giving 2n assignments by the rule of product. With three labels, the counts by number of red labels are 1,3,3,1, totalling eight. Choosing only the two group sizes would give the four possibilities (0,3),(1,2),(2,1),(3,0); it would forget which labels are red.
Indeed, the ordinary generating function for the constant sequence an​=1 is the geometric series 1/(1−z). Its square has coefficient [zn](1−z)−2=n+1, counting pairs of nonnegative sizes. Both encodings are correct for their respective questions. The decision is whether identity matters when objects are combined.
For unordered sets of labelled components of positive size, an exponential generating function B(z) becomes eB(z): the term B(z)m/m! forgets the ordering of m components. The existing rooted-tree generating function develops the richer example T=zeT. A labelled rooted tree consists of its root of a tree and an unordered set of smaller labelled rooted trees, connecting the same label-distribution mechanism to recursive counting.

Radius of convergence (R)

Words: 1k Articles: 12
Power series OurBigBook.com
The radius of convergence of ∑n≥0​an​(z−c)n is the unique R∈[0,∞] separating interior absolute convergence from exterior divergence. It converges absolutely when ∣z−c∣<R and diverges when ∣z−c∣>R. At the centre it always has the finite value a0​, since all positive powers vanish. The boundary convergence of a power series is a separate question.
For 0<R<∞, the interior is a disk in the complex plane and an open interval (c−R,c+R) on the real line. A power series converges uniformly on every smaller closed disk ∣z−c∣≤r<R. This gives stable polynomial approximation over a whole compact region, rather than a separate limiting calculation at each point. See Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis, §11.3.2: convergence of power series.
Four examples reveal what R measures:
  • ∑n≥0​zn has R=1, since its coefficients have constant magnitude one.
  • ∑n≥1​zn/n also has R=1: a factor 1/n changes boundary behaviour without changing the limiting coefficient-root growth.
  • ∑n≥0​zn/n! has R=∞. The ratio test gives successive term ratio ∣z∣/(n+1)→0 for every fixed z, producing the exponential function.
  • ∑n≥0​n!zn has R=0. For any z=0, successive term magnitudes have ratio (n+1)∣z∣→∞, so the terms do not tend to zero.
The Cauchy-Hadamard theorem computes R directly from the coefficients. The attractive feature is that one growth statistic decides convergence throughout the interior and exterior, including sparse series with many zero coefficients. Finite changes to the coefficients do not alter the radius, though they can change the sum.

Radius of a Maclaurin series from successive derivatives (R=limn→∞​​(n+1)f(n)(0)/f(n+1)(0)​)

Words: 90
Radius of convergence OurBigBook.com
Write the Maclaurin series coefficients as an​=f(n)(0)/n!. When the successive ratios exist eventually and have a limit, the ratio test gives the displayed radius of convergence, including zero and infinity. The unconditional formula is R−1=limsupn→∞​∣an​∣1/n, from the Cauchy-Hadamard theorem. Endpoints must be checked separately.
The existence and convergence of this power series do not by themselves imply that it equals f: equality requires analyticity or control of the Taylor remainder. The smooth function f(x)=e−1/x2 for x=0, f(0)=0, has all derivatives zero at zero, so its Maclaurin series is identically zero despite the nonzero values away from zero.

Isolating a logarithmic singularity to test a power-series endpoint (f(z)=Alog(1−z/R)+H(z))

Words: 135
Radius of convergence OurBigBook.com
Suppose A=0 and R>0, and H is an analytic function on a disk of radius strictly larger than R. The Taylor series at zero of f(z)=Alog(1−z/R)+H(z) has radius of convergence R. Its coefficients are the sum of −A/(nRn) and the more rapidly decreasing coefficients of H. At x=−R, the logarithmic part is an alternating harmonic series and converges conditionally; at x=R it diverges. The power series for H converges absolutely at both endpoints and therefore cannot change either conclusion. The real convergence interval is [−R,R).
For f(z)=log(2−ez), take R=log2 and H(z)=log[(2−ez)/(1−z/R)], with its branch normalized by H(0)=0. The quotient has nonzero removable value 2R at z=R. Its next zeros are at R±2πi, so a holomorphic logarithm exists on a larger disk. This shows why the Taylor series converges at x=−log2 even though its singular positive endpoint is excluded.

Radius of convergence OurBigBook.com
Knowing the radius of convergence does not settle convergence on its boundary. The three power series
∑n=0∞​zn,∑n=1∞​nzn​,∑n=1∞​n2zn​

all have radius one, but behave differently on ∣z∣=1.
For the geometric series, boundary terms all have complex modulus one, violating the term test for divergence. For the second series, absolute values give the divergent harmonic series at every boundary point. At z=1 the series itself is harmonic and diverges. At any other point on the unit circle, its geometric partial sums obey
​∑k=1N​zk​=​1−zz(1−zN)​​≤∣1−z∣2​.
(62)
The Dirichlet test with the decreasing sequence 1/n→0 therefore gives conditional convergence. In particular, z=−1 gives the negative of the alternating harmonic series, with sum −ln2. For the third series, the convergent p-series ∑n≥1​1/n2 bounds the absolute values at every boundary point, giving absolute convergence by the comparison test for series.
At z=−1, the rational function 1/(1−z) is well defined and equals 1/2, yet its geometric series diverges there. A formula for a function and a particular series representation can have different domains. Likewise, applying termwise differentiation of a power series preserves the radius but need not preserve the boundary convergence.

Away from the centre, the root test explains the formula: the limit superior of the term roots at displacement z−c is ∣z−c∣/R, interpreted as zero for R=∞ and infinite for R=0. Values below one give absolute convergence; values above one imply that the terms fail to tend to zero. A value of one leaves the boundary question open. At the centre the series converges regardless of R.
For a2n​=1 and a2n+1​=0, the coefficient roots alternate between one and zero, so their ordinary limit does not exist. Their limit superior is nevertheless one, giving R=1 for ∑n≥0​z2n=1/(1−z2) inside the unit disk. A ratio of consecutive coefficients would be undefined at the zero coefficients; the root-limsup formula handles the gap directly.
In the first part of his 1892 study of functions given by Taylor series, Jacques Hadamard introduced an upper-limit formulation for sequences and used coefficient roots to determine the radius of convergence. Sections 4–6 separate finite positive, zero, and infinite root-growth cases; the later parts study singularities and continuation. See Hadamard, Essai sur l'étude des fonctions données par leur développement de Taylor, Journal de mathématiques pures et appliquées, fourth series 8 (1892), pp. 107–109. This original text explains the coefficient-growth question without implying that the study of power series began there.

For a real-valued analytic function of a real variable, an even integer m gives the same nearby sign on both sides of c, while an odd integer m gives opposite signs. For example, f(x)=x2(1+x) has leading Taylor term x2 and is positive on both sides of zero sufficiently nearby; g(x)=x3(1+x) has leading Taylor term x3 and changes sign there. Words: 1k Articles: 13
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
A sequence of functions fn​:X→Y converges uniformly to f:X→Y, where Y is a metric space with metric d, precisely when
∀ε>0∃N∈N>0​∀x∈X∀n≥N:d(fn​(x),f(x))<ε.
(71)
For real numbers, use the absolute value d(u,v)=∣u−v∣. Compare the universal quantification and existential quantification:
pointwise:uniform:​∀x∀ε>0∃N∀n≥N,∀ε>0∃N∀x∀n≥N.​
(72)
The decisive change is whether N can depend on x. Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence.[ref]
For functions taking values in real numbers on a nonempty domain of a function, the supremum error is En​=supx∈X​∣fn​(x)−f(x)∣, allowing +∞. Then uniform convergence is equivalent to En​→0. The supremum need not be a maximum: pointwise strict bounds below ε only give En​≤ε, so use tolerance ε/2 when proving this equivalence. This single error bound controls every possible input, including one chosen after seeing the index.
For fn​(x)=xn and its pointwise limit on [0,1], the error is zero at one but approaches one as x→1 from below. Consequently
En​=supx∈[0,1]​∣fn​(x)−f(x)∣=1
(73)
for every positive integer n. This supremum is never attained: below one the error is xn<1, and at one it is zero. Deleting the endpoint leaves the same supremum error on [0,1). To disprove uniform convergence directly, choose ε=1/2: for any proposed N, take n=N and x=2−1/N<1. The error equals 1/2, violating the strict tolerance. Thus a moving input defeats every proposed common threshold.
On the smaller interval [0,a], for a fixed 0≤a<1, the pointwise limit is zero and
En​=maxx∈[0,a]​xn=an⟶0.
(74)
For 0<a<1 and 0<ε<1, the exact first successful common threshold is
N(a,ε)=⌊logalogε​⌋+1.
(75)
The logarithm and floor function turn an infinite approximation statement into a finite stopping rule. At a=0.8, 0.820=0.01152921504606846976 fails tolerance 0.01, while 0.821=0.009223372036854775808 succeeds. At a=1/2 and ε=1/8, the ratio is exactly three: N=4 is necessary because equality is insufficient. For a=0, every error is zero. The domain of a function determines whether one threshold can certify every input.
For another explicit stopping rule, let hn​(x)=x/(n+1) on [0,1]. Its uniform limit is zero and its supremum error is 1/(n+1). For every ε>0, N=max{1,⌈1/ε⌉} works, using the ceiling function. Unlike xn on [0,1], it controls even the endpoint.
The practical beauty of uniform convergence is that one quantitative bound can survive further operations: the uniform limit theorem preserves continuity, and uniform convergence preserves integrals on a compact interval controls accumulated error. Differentiation needs additional hypotheses, such as uniform derivative convergence with an anchored value. These results distinguish an approximation that looks accurate at selected inputs from one that justifies replacing a whole function in a calculation.

Cauchy sequence (∀ε>0∃N∀m,n≥N: d(xm​,xn​)<ε)

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
A Cauchy sequence is a sequence whose sufficiently late terms are all close to one another. In a metric space (X,d), the precise condition is
∀ε>0∃N∈N>0​∀m,n≥N: d(xm​,xn​)<ε.
(93)
For real numbers with their usual metric, d(xm​,xn​)=∣xm​−xn​∣. The useful feature is that the definition compares computed terms to other computed terms: it does not require an already known limit of a sequence. The one index N must control every pair of later indices, not merely successive terms. [ref].
For an explicit example, take qn​=1−2−n for n≥1. Its tail of a sequence beginning at N lies in [1−2−N,1), and for every m,n≥N,
∣qm​−qn​∣=∣2−n−2−m∣<2−N.
(94)
Choose N with 2−N<ε to certify the entire future sequence. For ε=0.1, N=4 works because 2−4=0.0625. The limit of a sequence is one, but the pairwise bound establishes the Cauchy sequence property without first needing that answer. By contrast, an​=(−1)n is not a Cauchy sequence: arbitrarily late even integers and odd integers give values separated by two. [ref].
Tiny successive changes do not provide this guarantee. For the harmonic numbers Hn​=∑j=1n​1/j, the successive difference Hn+1​−Hn​=1/(n+1) tends to zero, but
H2n​−Hn​=∑j=n+12n​j1​≥n2n1​=21​.
(95)
Thus, beyond every proposed N, choosing n≥N and m=2n defeats the fixed tolerance ε=1/2. Even every fixed positive lag h passes the weaker test: 0<Hn+h​−Hn​≤h/(n+1)→0. The failing lag grows with n, as explained more generally by convergence from arbitrary variable-lag increments. [ref].
Every convergent sequence in a metric space is a Cauchy sequence: apply the triangle inequality to two late terms and their common limit of a sequence. The reverse implication requires completeness. It holds in the real numbers by completeness of the real numbers, but can fail in the rational numbers: the rational endpoints from the bisection method approaching 2​ are a Cauchy sequence with no rational limit of a sequence. The existing construction in completeness of the real numbers shows how this happens. A Cauchy sequence is always a bounded sequence; in R, boundedness gives a convergent subsequence by the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, and the pairwise condition forces the whole sequence to share its limit. [ref].

Completeness of the real numbers

Words: 478 Articles: 2
Cauchy sequence OurBigBook.com
Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers converges to a real number. Explicitly, the condition
∀ε>0∃N∈N>0​∀m,n≥N:∣xm​−xn​∣<ε

implies the existence of L∈R with xn​→L. The hypothesis compares approximations with one another, without requiring a candidate answer. This makes completeness of the real numbers an existence principle: sufficiently consistent approximations cannot approach a missing destination. [ref].
The equivalent least-upper-bound property says that every nonempty set A⊆R bounded above has a supremum s∈R. Precisely, every x∈A satisfies x≤s, and for every ε>0 some x∈A satisfies s−ε<x. The second condition excludes any smaller upper bound. No largest element of A is required.
The rational numbers lack this property. The set A={q∈Q:q≥0, q2<2} contains one and has upper bound two, but has no supremum in Q. A proposed rational supremum s would have to satisfy s2=2: if s2<2, a sufficiently small rational increase still lies in A; if s2>2, a sufficiently small rational decrease remains an upper bound. The irrationality of the square root of two excludes equality. In R, its supremum is 2​. [ref].
Construct this square root by the bisection method, starting with rational bounds [l0​,u0​]=[1,2]. At each step square the midpoint and retain the half whose endpoints bracket two after squaring. The first four resulting intervals are [1,3/2], [5/4,3/2], [11/8,3/2], and [11/8,23/16]. After k steps, uk​−lk​=2−k and lk2​<2<uk2​. Both endpoint sequences are Cauchy sequences because every later endpoint remains in the current interval. Completeness of the real numbers gives a common limit of a sequence L; continuity of squaring gives L2=2. The midpoint approximates L with error at most 2−(k+1). Thus exact rational arithmetic produces certified accuracy while completeness of the real numbers supplies the exact answer.
Richard Dedekind approached completeness of the real numbers by filling gaps in the rational numbers with Dedekind cuts. In the preface to his 1872 Continuity and Irrational Numbers, he traced the problem to teaching differential calculus in 1858 and wanting arithmetic foundations for limits. His construction makes a missing boundary, such as 2​, into a number defined by the separation it produces among rational numbers. [ref].

Dedekind cut (A⊊Q)

Words: 118
Completeness of the real numbers OurBigBook.com
A Dedekind cut can be represented by a nonempty proper subset A of the rational numbers satisfying two conditions: if q∈A and r<q is rational, then r∈A; and A has no maximum. The complementary set contains all the rational values on the other side of the boundary. Using the convention that the lower set never includes its boundary avoids two representations of a rational boundary.
The set {q∈Q:q<0} represents zero. The set {q∈Q:q<0 or q2<2} represents 2​, even though no rational number occupies that boundary by the irrationality of the square root of two. Thus a Dedekind cut describes an irrational number entirely using rational comparisons. Ordering these cuts by the subset relation and defining their arithmetic gives a construction of the real numbers. [ref].

Least-upper-bound property

Words: 28
Completeness of the real numbers OurBigBook.com
The least-upper-bound property states that every nonempty set of real numbers that has an upper bound has a supremum in the real numbers. It is an order-theoretic formulation of the completeness of the real numbers.

Conditional convergence

Words: 197 Articles: 4
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
A series is conditionally convergent when it converges but does not converge absolutely.

Paired logarithmic series with zero sum (∑n=2∞​ln[1+(−1)n/n]=0)

Words: 80
Conditional convergence OurBigBook.com
The terms at n=2j and n=2j+1 are ln[(2j+1)/(2j)] and its negative. Thus the partial sums ending at an odd index are zero, while those ending at 2m equal ln[(2m+1)/(2m)]→0. Considering both subsequences proves convergence of the full sequence of partial sums, not merely of grouped terms.
The paired sum of absolute values is 2ln[1+1/(2j)]. Since ln(1+u)≥u/(1+u) for u≥0, these pairs dominate 2/(2j+1), whose series diverges by comparison with the harmonic series. The original series therefore has conditional convergence with the displayed sum.

Riemann series theorem

Words: 96 Articles: 1
Conditional convergence OurBigBook.com
A conditionally convergent real series can be rearranged to converge to any prescribed real value or to diverge. Its positive and negative subseries have infinite total magnitudes: successively add positive terms to cross a desired value and negative terms to cross back. Since the terms tend to zero, the overshoots shrink to zero.

Rearrangement of a series

Words: 44
Riemann series theorem OurBigBook.com
A rearrangement changes the order of a series without changing its multiset of terms. A conditionally convergent real series can be rearranged to approach any prescribed real limit or to diverge.
The Riemann series theorem specifies the possible sums of rearrangements of a conditionally convergent real series.

Alternating series test

Words: 8
Conditional convergence OurBigBook.com
If an​≥0 decreases to zero, then ∑n=1∞​(−1)nan​ converges.

P-series

Words: 154 Articles: 2
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
The series ∑n=1∞​n−p converges exactly when p>1.

Shifted integral representation of a p-series tail (kp​=N−[(p−1)∑n=N∞​n−p]−1/(p−1))

Words: 87
P-series OurBigBook.com
Fix an integer N>1 and a real exponent p>1, and put Sp​=∑n=N∞​n−p. There is a unique shift kp​<N such that
∫N∞​(x−kp​)−pdx=Sp​.
(97)
Integration evaluates the left side as (N−kp​)1−p/(p−1), yielding the displayed formula. Comparing the decreasing function x−p with unit rectangles proves
p−1N1−p​<Sp​<p−1(N−1)1−p​.
(98)
The integral is a strictly increasing function of its shift, so 0<kp​<1. This is an exact reparametrization of a tail, not a claim that its shift is independent of p; interpolating shifts for different exponents is an additional approximation.

Telescoping bound for a p-series (∑n=1N​n−k≤1+[1−N−(k−1)]/(k−1),k>1)

Words: 59
P-series OurBigBook.com
For p>0 and n≥2, integrating the decreasing derivative magnitude of x−p gives (n−1)−p−n−p=p∫n−1n​x−p−1dx>pn−p−1. Put p=k−1 and sum this telescoping series to obtain the bound in the title, strict for N>1. The partial sums are increasing and bounded, proving convergence of the p-series when k>1. This gives a direct comparison test for series proof and a finite upper bound without evaluating the sum.

Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
A series converges absolutely when the series of absolute values converges; absolute convergence implies convergence.

Squares of a summable positive sequence

Absolute convergence OurBigBook.com
If an​≥0 and ∑an​<∞, then an​→0, so eventually an2​≤an​ and ∑an2​ converges.

Geometric means of two summable positive sequences

Words: 5
Absolute convergence OurBigBook.com
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives
∑n​an​bn​​≤(∑n​an​)1/2(∑n​bn​)1/2.
(99)

Weighted square roots of a summable sequence

Words: 26
Absolute convergence OurBigBook.com
If an​≥0, ∑an​<∞, and p>1/2, then
∑n​an​​n−p≤(∑n​an​)1/2(∑n​n−2p)1/2<∞.
(100)
The endpoint can fail: an​=1/(n(logn)2) gives the divergent series ∑1/(nlogn).

Total variation

Words: 154 Articles: 2
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
The total variation of a sequence is ∑n​∣an+1​−an​∣; convergence alone does not make it finite.

Total generalized variation (TGVα2​)

Words: 138 Articles: 1
Total variation OurBigBook.com
Second-order total generalized variation combines a first derivative with an auxiliary vector field and its symmetric derivative. A standard continuous form is
TGVα2​(u)=infw​{α1​∥Du−w∥M​+α0​∥Ew∥M​},α0​,α1​>0.
(101)
Here Ew denotes the symmetric distributional derivative and the norms are total variations of the corresponding measures. Discrete variants replace these operators by linear maps and use sums of row norms. Unlike first-order total variation, this regularizer accommodates piecewise-affine behavior. A TGV divergence splitting makes its constrained divergence dual amenable to explicit proximal operators.

TGV divergence splitting

Words: 64
Total generalized variation OurBigBook.com
For a quadratic data term and divergence maps A1​,A2​, the dual constraint A1​v∈D can be split through δD​(A1​v)=supw​[⟨w,A1​v⟩−δD∗​(w)]. For a product of Euclidean row balls of radius β, its support function is δD∗​(w)=β∑i​∥wi​∥2​. The resulting saddle coupling is K(u,w)=A2∗​u−A1∗​w. The Chambolle–Pock algorithm then uses a row-ball projection, a quadratic proximal operator and radial soft thresholding, with no projection onto an intersection involving a divergence operator.

Harmonic sums satisfy ∑j=n+12n​1/j→log2 by integral comparison.

Convergent series

Words: 608 Articles: 14
Sequence and series OurBigBook.com
A series converges when its sequence of partial sums converges to a finite limit.

Terms of a convergent series tend to zero (∑n=1∞​un​ converges ⟹ un​→0)

Words: 37
Convergent series OurBigBook.com
If the partial sums Sn​=∑j=1n​uj​ tend to a finite limit S, then un​=Sn​−Sn−1​→S−S=0. Thus failure of the terms to tend to zero proves divergence. The converse is false: the harmonic series has terms tending to zero but diverges.

Convergence from fixed-length series blocks (bn​=∑j=1m​am(n−1)+j​)

Words: 74
Convergent series OurBigBook.com
For a fixed positive integer m, if an​→0 and the series of the displayed block sums converges, then the original series converges to the same limit of a sequence. Its partial sum at a block endpoint is exactly a partial sum of ∑bn​; the difference at an intermediate endpoint has at most m−1 terms, all tending to zero. This justification is essential when block cancellation proves convergence without absolute convergence. It does not apply without further control to blocks whose lengths grow.

Dirichlet test

Words: 84
Convergent series OurBigBook.com
If the partial sums of ∑bn​ are bounded and an​ decreases to zero, then ∑an​bn​ converges. The uniform version holds for functions bn​(x) when their partial sums have one bound M independent of x. Indeed partial sums starting at index N have absolute value at most 2M, and summation by parts bounds every weighted tail from N to K by 2MaN​. The uniformly Cauchy sequence criterion proves uniform convergence. This justifies integrating a conditionally convergent Fourier series on intervals staying away from its endpoint jump.

Comparison test for series

Words: 230 Articles: 4
Convergent series OurBigBook.com
For nonnegative sequences with 0≤an​≤bn​, convergence of ∑n​bn​ implies convergence of ∑n​an​, while divergence of ∑n​an​ implies divergence of ∑n​bn​.

Ratio comparison test (an+1​/an​≤bn+1​/bn​)

Words: 60
Comparison test for series OurBigBook.com
For positive sequences (an​),(bn​), suppose an+1​/an​≤bn+1​/bn​ eventually. Then an​/bn​ is eventually nonincreasing, so an​≤Cbn​ beyond a fixed index. The comparison test for series proves convergence of ∑an​ whenever ∑bn​ converges. Reversing the ratio inequality gives an eventual lower bound an​≥cbn​ and hence divergence when the positive comparison series diverges. The initial finite set of terms does not affect either conclusion.

Clipping preserves divergence of a positive series (∑n​xn​=∞⟹∑n​min(xn​,c)=∞)

Words: 51
Comparison test for series OurBigBook.com
If xn​>0 and c>0, clipping every term at c preserves divergence. If infinitely many terms are at least c, the clipped series has infinitely many terms equal to c and diverges. Otherwise its tail agrees with the original series. This lemma is useful in proving convergence from minimum-decrement inequalities.

Integral test for convergence

Words: 94 Articles: 1
Comparison test for series OurBigBook.com
If f:[1,∞)→[0,∞) is decreasing, then ∑n≥1​f(n) and ∫1∞​f(x)dx either both converge or both diverge. This follows by bounding the area under the graph between adjacent upper and lower rectangle sums.
Integral comparison for a nonincreasing nonnegative function (∫1N+1​f(x)dx≤∑n=1N​f(n)≤f(1)+∫1N​f(x)dx)
Words: 63
Integral test for convergence OurBigBook.com
For a nonnegative nonincreasing function f:[1,∞)→[0,∞), comparison with unit-width rectangles gives
∫1N+1​f(x)dx≤∑n=1N​f(n)≤f(1)+∫1N​f(x)dx.
(102)
On [n,n+1], the function is at most f(n); on [n−1,n], it is at least f(n). Summing these inequalities gives the bounds. Applying them to f(x)=1/x gives log(N+1)≤HN​≤1+logN for the harmonic numbers. Unlike a convergence verdict alone, the finite bounds estimate the size of a partial sum.

Ratio test OurBigBook.com
Suppose an​>0 and, for all sufficiently large n, an+1​/an​≤1−c/n with fixed c>0. Choose an initial index N>c. Since log(1−x)≤−x for 0<x<1, summing logarithmic ratios gives log(an​/aN​)≤−c∑k=Nn−1​1/k≤−clog(n/N). Thus an​≤aN​Ncn−c. For c>1, the comparison test for series with a P-series proves convergence. This supplies a useful refinement when a limiting ratio of one makes the ordinary ratio test inconclusive.
